result: ADSL is a conserved homotetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the eighth reaction in de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) and participates in the purine nucleotide cycle.
evaluation: Claims C1, C14, and C15 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019) and the schematic in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. These are established facts about ADSL function.

result: Mutations in ADSL cause ADSLD, an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defects in purine metabolism and heterogeneous neurological phenotypes including microcephaly and autism spectrum disorder. Over 100 patients have been diagnosed to date.
evaluation: Claims C2, C16, C17, and C18 are supported by multiple citations to clinical literature (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015) and represent well-established clinical knowledge about ADSLD.

result: ADSLD patients have normal serum purine nucleotide levels but exhibit accumulation of dephosphorylated ADSL substrates (S-Ado and SAICAr), which has been proposed to play a role in disease pathology.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C19, C20, and C21 are supported by citations to clinical observations (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015; Stone et al., 1998). These represent established clinical findings in ADSLD patients.

result: In model organisms (yeast and C. elegans), ADSL loss causes lethality, genomic instability, and developmental defects. In yeast, lethality can be rescued by deleting upstream DNPS enzymes, indicating that metabolite accumulation rather than impaired DNPS underlies toxicity.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by citations to studies in yeast (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Giaever et al., 2002; Pinson et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2016) and C. elegans (Chen et al., 2016; Marsac et al., 2019; Fenton et al., 2017). These represent established findings from prior work.

result: SAICAr has been implicated in neurotoxic effects through unknown mechanisms. In rat brains, SAICAr perfusion caused hippocampal cellular attrition. In cancer cells, SAICAR accumulation activates PKM2 and other kinases.
evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by citations to prior studies (Stone et al., 1998; Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016). These represent established findings from the literature, though the mechanisms remain speculative.

result: ADSL depletion in RPE-1 cells resulted in 80% mRNA depletion, reduced protein levels, decreased AMP and GMP levels, and accumulation of S-Ado. SAICAr levels were at the limit of detection in RPE-1 cells but elevated in HeLa cells.
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by qRT-PCR (Figure 1A), Western blot (Figure 1B), and LC-MS data (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C). The data demonstrate effective ADSL depletion and expected metabolic changes.

result: ADSL depletion in RPE-1 cells reduced proliferation, caused loss of Ki67 expression, increased p53 levels, and resulted in G1 accumulation without increasing cell death or senescence.
evaluation: Claims C37-C42 are supported by cell counting (Figure 1D), immunofluorescence (Figure 1E-F), flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), Trypan Blue assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), and β-galactosidase assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G). The data consistently demonstrate cell cycle effects without cell death.

result: The cell cycle defects in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells were rescued by TP53 deletion or expression of siRNA-resistant ADSL. ADSL-depleted cells did not undergo differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by cell counting and flow cytometry data (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2H-I), immunofluorescence rescue experiments (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2J), and differentiation marker staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K). The rescue experiments provide strong evidence for specificity.

result: Nucleoside supplementation or PAICS inhibition did not prevent p53 induction or cell cycle exit in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells, indicating a p53-dependent cell cycle arrest not rescued by these interventions.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing lack of rescue by nucleosides (Figure 1I-J) or PAICS inhibitor (Figure 1K-L). This demonstrates that the cell cycle phenotype is distinct from DNA damage or metabolite accumulation effects.

result: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells showed increased chromatin-bound RPA levels (indicative of replication stress) and increased 53BP1 foci (indicative of DNA double-strand breaks). 53BP1 foci were reduced by ATM inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased RPA2 (Figure 2A), increased 53BP1 foci (Figure 2B), and ATM inhibitor rescue (Figure 2C). The data demonstrate mild DNA damage signaling with an active DNA damage response.

result: DNA damage signaling in ADSL-depleted cells was suppressed by nucleoside or adenosine supplementation but not by PAICS inhibition, implicating defects in the purine nucleotide cycle rather than impaired DNPS.
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing nucleoside rescue of 53BP1 foci (Figure 2D-F) and γH2AX (Figure 2G), but no rescue by PAICS inhibitor (Figure 2H). The differential rescue pattern provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

result: The p53-dependent cell cycle exit in ADSL-depleted cells is not solely a consequence of DNA damage signaling or purine metabolite accumulation.
evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by the lack of rescue of cell cycle exit by nucleosides or PAICS inhibition (Figure 1I-L), despite these interventions rescuing DNA damage. This indicates involvement of additional pathways.

result: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes reduced both SOX2-positive neural progenitors and ELAVL3/4-positive neurons, resulting in smaller tissue size without increased apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by qRT-PCR confirming depletion (Figure 3A), immunofluorescence showing reduced cell populations (Figure 3B), and cleaved caspase-3 staining showing no increase in apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The data demonstrate in vivo effects on neurogenesis.

result: Within GFP-positive transfected cells in chicken neural tubes, ADSL depletion increased the percentage of SOX2-positive progenitors relative to ELAVL3/4-positive neurons, with a slight increase in G2/M population, suggesting a proliferation defect rather than premature differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by immunofluorescence analysis of transfected cells (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and FACS analysis (Figure 3D). The data support impaired proliferation rather than altered differentiation.

result: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes caused reduced EdU incorporation, increased pH3S10-positive cells (specifically in G2 phase), indicating a G2 delay. In vivo, ADSL depletion leads to reduced cellularity without clear cell death or senescence.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by EdU incorporation and pH3S10 staining (Figure 3E-F). The separation of G2 and mitotic pH3S10 populations provides strong evidence for a specific G2 delay. The conclusion integrates in vitro and in vivo findings.

result: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells had fewer and shorter cilia after serum starvation. The ciliogenesis defect was not simply delayed, as similar defects were observed at 72 hr.
evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced cilia number and length (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B). The time course experiment rules out a simple delay.

result: Ciliogenesis defects in ADSL-depleted cells were rescued by siRNA-resistant ADSL expression or MTX/PAICS inhibitor treatment, but not by nucleoside supplementation.
evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing rescue by ADSL* (Figure 4C), no rescue by nucleosides (Figure 4D), no effect of MTX on control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), rescue by MTX in ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and rescue by PAICS inhibitor (Figure 4E). The differential rescue pattern is consistent and well-documented.

result: SAICAr treatment phenocopied the ciliogenesis defect without activating AKT. The defect was independent of p53 status and cilia removal kinetics were normal, indicating that impaired DNPS at the ADSL step and/or SAICAr accumulation impairs ciliogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are supported by SAICAr treatment data (Figure 4F-G), Western blot showing no AKT activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), p53 KO experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), and cilia removal kinetics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G). The comprehensive controls strengthen the conclusion.

result: ADSL depletion impaired CP110 removal from the mother centriole, which could be phenocopied by SAICAr and rescued by PAICS inhibition or CP110 co-depletion, but not by nucleoside supplementation.
evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by immunofluorescence showing normal centrosomes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), impaired CP110 removal (Figure 5B), SAICAr phenocopy (Figure 5C), PAICS inhibitor rescue (Figure 5D), and CP110 co-depletion rescue (Figure 5E). The data identify a specific mechanistic step in ciliogenesis.

result: Adsl is ubiquitously expressed in early zebrafish embryos and highly expressed in the developing brain by the 18-somite stage. Morpholino injection abolished Adsl expression in neurons.
evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are supported by in situ hybridization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-L) and immunofluorescence (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The data demonstrate expression pattern and effective depletion.

result: Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos displayed pericardial edema, kinked tail, hydrocephalus, and microcephaly phenotypes. Nearly 50% exhibited defects in skull formation, which could be rescued by zebrafish or human ADSL but not by the R426H mutant.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by live imaging (Figure 6A-E) and Alcian Blue staining (Figure 6F). The rescue experiments with wild-type but not mutant ADSL provide strong evidence for specificity and relevance to human disease.

result: Adsl depletion in zebrafish increased γH2AX-positive cells in the neural tube, which was suppressed by nucleoside treatment, demonstrating DNA damage that could be suppressed with nucleoside supplementation.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6G). The nucleoside rescue in zebrafish parallels the findings in RPE-1 cells, strengthening the overall conclusion.

result: Adsl-depleted zebrafish showed heart looping defects, inverse liver placement, and altered spaw mRNA localization (about 40% with symmetric or absent staining), which could be largely restored by zebrafish Adsl expression.
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by in situ hybridization for cmcl2 (Figure 7A), angptl3 (Figure 7B), and spaw (Figure 7C). The rescue experiments demonstrate specificity. These phenotypes are consistent with ciliary defects.

result: In the Kupffer's vesicle, Adsl depletion did not significantly affect KV area or cilia number but reduced cilia length, which was partially rescued by zebrafish Adsl expression. Combined with laterality defects and hydrocephalus, this supports a role for ADSL in cilia formation or function in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by confocal microscopy data (Figure 7D-G). The specific effect on cilia length without affecting number or KV area is consistent with the in vitro findings. The integration with other ciliopathy phenotypes strengthens the conclusion.

result: Adsl depletion in zebrafish reduced Elavl3/4-positive cells, which was rescued by zebrafish Adsl expression or MTX treatment, indicating that the reduction was due to metabolite accumulation rather than impaired DNPS per se.
evaluation: Claims C107-C111 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced Elavl3/4+ cells (Figure 8A), rescue by Adsl expression (Figure 8A), complete rescue by MTX (Figure 8B), and replication with a second morpholino (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The MTX rescue is particularly strong evidence for the metabolite accumulation hypothesis.

result: Adsl depletion reduced Sox2-positive neural progenitors in zebrafish, which was rescued by MTX but not by nucleoside supplementation, indicating a specific role of impaired DNPS and likely SAICAr accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C112-C115 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced Sox2+ cells (Figure 8C), rescue by MTX (Figure 8C), and no rescue by nucleosides (Figure 8D). The differential rescue pattern provides strong mechanistic insight.

result: Diminished AMP levels from ADSL depletion result in DNA damage signaling and cell cycle delays (rescued by nucleosides), while ciliogenesis defects are specifically caused by loss of ADSL or SAICAr administration (rescued by PAICS/MTX inhibition but not nucleosides). Both reduced purine levels and impaired DNPS contribute to neurodevelopmental pathology.
evaluation: Claims C6, C12, C116-C119 represent the major integrative conclusion of the manuscript. They are supported by the comprehensive differential rescue experiments throughout Figures 1-8. The consistent pattern of nucleoside rescue for DNA damage but not ciliogenesis, and PAICS/MTX rescue for ciliogenesis but not DNA damage, provides strong evidence for pathway-specific effects.

result: Primary ciliogenesis is impaired by ADSL loss or SAICAr administration. ADSL-deficient chicken and zebrafish embryos displayed impaired neurogenesis and microcephaly. Neuroprogenitor attrition in zebrafish was rescued by DNPS inhibition but not nucleotides. Zebrafish displayed ciliopathy phenotypes. Defective ciliogenesis may influence the ADSLD phenotypic spectrum.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11, C13 represent the major findings from the abstract. They are supported by extensive data in Figures 3-8 showing ciliogenesis defects (Figures 4-5, 7), neurogenesis defects (Figures 3, 8), microcephaly (Figures 3, 6), differential rescue by MTX vs nucleosides (Figures 8), and ciliopathy phenotypes (Figures 6-7). The evidence is comprehensive and consistent across multiple model systems.

result: Microcephaly was observed in zebrafish and chicken embryos following ADSL depletion, suggesting these are valuable models for understanding microcephaly etiology in ADSLD.
evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by data in Figures 3, 6, and 8 showing reduced brain/neural tube size in both model systems. The phenotype is consistent with clinical observations in ADSLD patients (cited literature). The models provide mechanistic insights not available from patient studies.

result: Despite phenotypic similarities with Seckel syndrome (DNA damage, p53 activation, cilia defects), ADSL depletion did not increase cell death, indicating a mechanistically distinct pathway from Seckel syndrome driven by ATR deficiency or centrosome duplication defects.
evaluation: Claims C125-C132 are supported by the lack of cell death in ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F) and comparison with cited literature on Seckel syndrome. The distinction is important for understanding ADSLD pathology and is well-supported by the data.

result: GMPS was identified as a p53 target and promotes p53 stabilization via USP7. However, this pathway likely does not explain p53 activation in ADSL depletion, as nucleosides did not rescue p53 activation and the GMPS pathway induces cell death.
evaluation: Claims C133-C135 are supported by citations to prior work (Holzer et al., 2017; Reddy et al., 2014) and the lack of nucleoside rescue of p53 (Figure 1I-J) and absence of cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F). The reasoning is sound.

result: Defects in cilium removal and premature differentiation have been implicated in microcephaly. However, ADSL-depleted cells showed normal cilia removal rates and no premature differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are supported by citations to prior work (Gabriel et al., 2016; Farooq et al., 2020) and data showing normal cilia removal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) and no differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K). This rules out these alternative mechanisms.

result: Cell cycle delays and reduced SOX2+ progenitors and ELAVL3/4+ neurons were observed in both chicken and zebrafish. The increase in transfected Sox2+ cells in chicken further supports cell cycle delay.
evaluation: Claims C139-C142 are supported by data in Figures 1, 3, and 8. The observation that transfected Sox2+ cells increase while overall Sox2+ cells decrease (Figure 3C) provides particularly strong evidence for cell cycle delay rather than cell death or differentiation.

result: Nutrient restriction arrests neural progenitors in G2 reversibly. Purine deficiency inhibits mTORC1, and mTORC1 inactivation causes microcephaly in mice mainly through cell death. While mTOR dysregulation cannot be ruled out, the origin of microcephaly in ADSLD is likely mechanistically distinct.
evaluation: Claims C143-C147 are supported by citations to prior work (McKeown and Cline, 2019; Hoxhaj et al., 2017; Cloëtta et al., 2013) and the lack of cell death in ADSL-depleted systems. The reasoning is sound and appropriately cautious.

result: The reduction in brain size from ADSL depletion is largely due to impaired cell cycle progression in SOX2-positive progenitors and delayed differentiation.
evaluation: Claim C148 is supported by the comprehensive data in Figures 3 and 8 showing G2 delay, reduced Sox2+ cells, and reduced Elavl3/4+ cells without increased cell death. This represents a major mechanistic conclusion of the manuscript.

result: The molecular targets of SAICAR remain unclear, but it has been linked to PKM2 and MYC activation in cancer. SAICAr could affect cilia through AKT/mTOR signaling, but SAICAr treatment did not increase AKT activation, indicating a distinct mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C149-C154 are supported by citations to prior work (Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016; Zurlo et al., 2019; Hoxhaj et al., 2017; Walia et al., 2019) and Western blot data showing no AKT activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E). The discussion appropriately acknowledges uncertainty while ruling out one mechanism.

result: ADSL has been identified as a proximal interactor of centrosomal proteins (CEP104, CEP128, CEP135, CEP152, CEP89, centrobin), suggesting it may play regulatory roles at centrosomes.
evaluation: Claims C155-C156 are supported by citation to prior work (Gupta et al., 2015). This represents an interesting hypothesis for future investigation but is not directly tested in this manuscript.

result: This is the first demonstration of a specific purine metabolite impairing ciliogenesis. While ciliopathy features have not been described in ADSLD, the robust rescue by MTX and observation of shorter cilia and ciliopathy phenotypes in zebrafish suggest SAICAr effects on cilia may be involved.
evaluation: Claims C157-C162 are supported by the comprehensive ciliogenesis data in Figures 4-7. The novelty claim (C157) appears reasonable given the literature review. The observation of ciliopathy phenotypes in zebrafish (Figures 6-7) combined with MTX rescue (Figure 8) provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

result: Primary cilia and Hedgehog signaling regulate brain progenitors. However, severe cilia/Hedgehog defects cause more drastic reductions than observed in ADSL-depleted systems, consistent with milder ciliogenesis effects in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C163-C164 are supported by citations to prior work (Bangs and Anderson, 2017; Breunig et al., 2008; Han et al., 2008) and comparison with the observed phenotypes. The reasoning is sound and appropriately cautious.

result: ADSL knockdown was used experimentally, and it is unclear to what extent ciliary defects would be recapitulated by ADSL mutations in patients. If deficiency is less severe or tissue-specific, patients may not present classic ciliopathy features.
evaluation: Claims C165-C166 represent appropriate caveats about the limitations of the study. The use of knockdown rather than patient mutations is a limitation, and the speculation about patient phenotypes is appropriately cautious.

result: The work provides cell-level analysis of ADSL deficiency, identifies specific cellular defects, ascribes them to specific DNPS or purine nucleotide cycle steps, adds support for SAICAr's role in pathology, and establishes a framework for deciphering molecular mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C167-C170 represent the overall conclusions of the manuscript. They are well-supported by the comprehensive data throughout Figures 1-8, particularly the differential rescue experiments that distinguish between purine nucleotide cycle and DNPS pathway effects.

result: SAICAr has been implicated in neurotoxic effects through unknown mechanisms. The underlying mechanisms by which neuropathology arises in ADSLD remain unknown.
evaluation: Claims C5, C21, C28, C30, C31 represent the knowledge gap that motivates the study. They are supported by citations to prior work (Stone et al., 1998; Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015) and accurately describe the state of the field.

result: SAICAr levels were barely detectable in RPE-1 cells, which could indicate that very small amounts are sufficient or that signaling from ADSL protein loss is responsible. p53 activation and cell cycle defects were insensitive to nucleosides or DNPS modulation, indicating additional pathways.
evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by the LC-MS data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and lack of rescue by nucleosides or PAICS inhibitor (Figure 1I-L). The speculation about mechanisms is appropriately cautious and acknowledges uncertainty.
